intro: Lyon protects its remarkable trees in law, and the Métropole surveys its street trees one by one. The Parc de la Tête d'Or, laid out from 1856 to rival Paris's Bois de Boulogne, holds the rarities, among them a Chinese lacebark pine. The measured giants stand outside it, a plane 5.78 metres round facing the Île Barbe, black poplars in Gerland, cedars and copper beeches on a Croix-Rousse square. Further out, Caluire, Bron, Écully and the Saône villages add a weeping blue cedar, planes never pruned and three the Métropole puts at over 150 years old.
meta_description: Lyon's remarkable trees, from an 1856 Chinese pine in the Tête d'Or to a 5.78 m plane on the Saône and a weeping blue cedar in Caluire. Where to find them.
question_meta: Lyon's most precisely dated remarkable tree is an 1856 Chinese pine in the Parc de la Tête d'Or. Where it stands, and 33 more trees.
question_answer: Lyon has no single documented oldest tree, but its most precisely dated remarkable tree is the Pin de Bunge, also called the Pin de Napoléon, in the Parc de la Tête d'Or, planted around 1856 during the park's creation and now roughly 170 years old. It carries France's national Arbre Remarquable label. The Métropole's register puts three planes on Quai Clemenceau in Caluire-et-Cuire at more than 150 years old, but gives them no planting date.
question_context: Lyon is one of the few cities with real published records to work from. The city keeps a list of trees holding the national Arbre Remarquable label, awarded by the A.R.B.R.E.S. association, and the Métropole publishes two more as open data, a register of protected remarkable trees under its planning rules and a survey of its street trees with girth, height and crown measured tree by tree. Those records favour rarity, size and documented planting over sheer age, which is why the Pin de Bunge, a Chinese species first introduced to Europe through Kew Gardens in the nineteenth century, still anchors the question. It stands on the perimeter path of the Tête d'Or arboretum, five minutes from the Boulevard des Belges entrance, in a park that holds France's Ensemble Arboré Remarquable label for its whole collection. The Métropole's register gives one written age elsewhere, more than 150 years for three planes on Quai Clemenceau in Caluire-et-Cuire, without a planting date. Most of the other big trees, including a plane 5.78 metres round on Quai Raoul Carrié, are measured but not dated.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lyon?
faq.a: No single tree in Lyon has a documented claim to be the oldest. The most precisely dated remarkable tree is the Pin de Bunge in Parc de la Tête d'Or, planted around 1856 during the park's creation and now roughly 170 years old. The Métropole's register puts three planes on Quai Clemenceau in Caluire-et-Cuire at more than 150 years old.

faq.q: Why does Parc de la Tête d'Or have so many rare trees?
faq.a: It was designed from 1856 by Swiss landscape architects Eugène and Denis Bühler as a full arboretum alongside a public park, and absorbed Lyon's old botanical garden collection in 1857, giving it species pulled from four continents rather than the usual local mix.

faq.q: How does Lyon protect its remarkable trees?
faq.a: Through the national Arbre Remarquable label, awarded by the A.R.B.R.E.S. association, which four individual Lyon trees currently hold, and through the Métropole's urban plan, the PLU-H, which protects individual remarkable trees by name and location, from the cedars of Square Ferrié to the unpruned planes of Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or.

faq.q: Are all of these trees in Lyon itself?
faq.a: Most are, but several stand in neighbouring communes of the Métropole, in Villeurbanne, Caluire-et-Cuire, Bron, Écully, Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or and Albigny-sur-Saône, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from the centre by public transport. From Square Ferrié on the Croix-Rousse plateau, Place de la Rochette and the church of Saint-Côme-Saint-Damien in Caluire are about a kilometre and a half on foot.

faq.q: Are Lyon's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. All of them are free to see with no entry fee, from the Tête d'Or arboretum to a plane on the Saône quay facing the Île Barbe and a rare oak on an ordinary Villeurbanne street corner.
